titleStmt.title: Interview with June Delay Tallent, n.d.
titleStmt.author: Michael Willie and Suzanne Trimble [transcriber]

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with June Delay Tallent was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: __ office Northgate Mall Chattanooga, Tennessee. Ms. Tallent was born on June 15, 1928, and is now 75 years old. My name is Michael Willie, and I'll conduct this interview. Ms. Tallent, could you state for the recording your name and its spelling, please?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: My name is June, J-u-n-e, Tallent, T-a-l-l-e-n-t.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Where were you born, Ms. Tallent?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: In Bradley County, Cleveland, Tennessee.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. Explain where that is in relation to, say, Chattanooga.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: It's about 30 miles--

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: --north of Chattanooga.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Now, you were born in Bradley County. Were you raised there, also?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Spend your formative years there?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you have any brothers and sisters?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: I had one brother.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Older or younger?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Younger.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Now, let's talk about your early years. You were born in 1928, and then did you say you lost your mother?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And when was that?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you were, what, 10, 11 years old?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Uh-huh. I think I was ten.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How did that effect the rest of your family, your father in particular?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Well, it affected a change in our lifestyle.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What did your father do for a living?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: He worked at Hardwick's Woollen Mill in Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And--

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: And--

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you say your brother was older or younger?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Younger.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. Then in 1940, talk about that day in November.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: My dad came home and informed my brother and myself and the housekeeper that we were moving across town with his mother, Grandmother Delay. And we were both unhappy because we had lived where we lived--that's the only home that I ever remember living in and had went through the six years of Mayfield Grammar School, and had just started in the 7th grade at Arnold School.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hm. All of your friends were there.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: All of my friends were there, and we were moving all the way across town, which to us as children, it was just miles and miles and miles, and the following week--we had moved over the weekend. The following week, I started to school at Allen School, and everybody was real nice. I met a girl that introduced herself at recess, who became my best friend for life, and we correspond today. She's in Florida, been there for years. But I--being unhappy as I was, I talked my dad into letting me go to work in the ice cream parlor that his friend had just built in 1942 onto his grocery store. I begged and pleaded. I didn't want to stay there and not have anything to do. So I had started talking as soon as I started in the 8th grade. And that Christmas, of course, we all were jolted when December the 7th we were getting ready for church and came on the radio about the bombing of Pearl Harbor. So my biggest concern was what effect it would have on my uncle who had had to go into the Army and was going to be back.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hm. And he had gone in a year earlier. Right?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: He went in. That's why we moved there with my grandmother because my uncle had to go into training. That was--there was a song out of "I'll be back in a year little darling." All of the boys went for training for a year, and they came home, just in case of war, and then they would be called back. But the bombing of Pearl Harbor happened before his actual year was to be up. And more than ever, then I wanted to go to work. So my dad came in one night and told me that he and Bill had talked about it, and I could go to work, just as soon as I graduated from the 8th grade, so I started to work there. That was on a trial basis. It ended up I worked every day after school all during high school. I learned the grocery business inside out. And in the meantime had met this boy, we were sweethearts, didn't date, who was the guy that I later married.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hm. So you continued in school. You were just working after school.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Oh, I graduated from high school, but I worked all during high school every afternoon. It was just a routine that by the year I started my freshman year in high school in 1942, everything was just talk of the war. It was just--we were just very, very concerned.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Were a lot of boys leaving from__--

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Yes, uh-huh. Cleveland, you could walk through the main square of Cleveland, and what used to be the hang out in the spot two or three places there in Cleveland, there would be just maybe a half a dozen boys. Even the guy that had run the spot for years, he had went in the Army. They just left right and left. So I really wanted to do something more than just work. I felt like I wasn't doing too much more than work. In high school, my best friend I had met there in grade school at Allen, we volunteered to help at the old spec hospital, and that counted as one of our classes while we were in high school. One of the boy's father managed F.W. Woolworth's there in Cleveland, and he came to school one day and said his dad was real short of help, and he thought of me and Marie, because my friend worked at another small grocery store in town, if we would help his dad out, particularly during the Christmas season, so I worked at Woolworth's two or three weeks, and then went from there to the store, and then up the next morning at school, never took a day off. We were at the store seven days a week; I was in school five days a week, thought no more about it than anything. But--

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: But did you see that everybody was really pitching in? Was there a sense that--

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: That's what I was going to tell you. My grandmother was a very religious person, and right after the bombing of Pearl Harbor, she gets her quilting frames out, and her missionary group--and I don't remember those quilting frames coming down until after the war. They donated to the Red Cross so many quilts a week. They pledged so many quilts because everything was so scarce that I've often wondered how many quilts that my grandmother's missionary society donated to the Red Cross.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Isn't that wonderful?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: And when President Roosevelt came out in one of his speeches that if everybody would cut down from buying so much--so many groceries and grow their own food, that much more could be sent to our boys overseas. So my grandmother had an extra lot at her house, and she had that plowed up into a--they had the biggest garden you have ever seen. She did any and everything that she could. They wrote boys. She got names from the Red Cross there in Cleveland. Their missionary society and the preacher, all of them sent letters to soldiers. She sent packages. They would work for days at the church getting packages up, doing 43 and 44 to send to the men in service. And my uncle was in the medical corps. The one that had went in for training, he was sent to India, and it was real hard to get things to those boys for some reason, and so she always had special, a special section of Uncle Van's things and his friends for the medical corps in India, which he stayed there until 1945. He came home in late 1945. He got home just before Christmas on furlough, then had to go back, and then was--got his discharge, and I still think he got his discharge before '46. I believe it was in late, late '45. But I think that everybody pitched in, and I know the store -- looking back now, the store is still there. It was a supermarket. I think my daddy's friend and my dad's heads together were far advanced because it had--I know when the store was finished in 1940, he got buggies for people to come buy their groceries, even though he had built the business on delivering groceries. Everything that was short was rationed. We got stamps from the government, and I never thought about it until years later, and I wondered well how they knew how many stamps to send, but they knew every family and how many was in the family, and I know that when we got our books of gasoline, meat, sugar, and other things, dad just took the whole books to the store, and they were deposited in the bank at the store. So when wholesale items were bought that were rationed and you had to give stamps to, they would write a check for the ration stamps, just like a check from the bank. Of course, they give the money on a different check, but merchants banks there in Cleveland came up with that idea for the business people to--the grocery men to deposit their food stamps--it's--I don't guess you would say food stamp--food ration stamps, but there was a lot sold on the black market, too, if you wanted to pay top dollar for a can of salmon or anything. But we had a great big basement in the store, and that's where our special things stayed, and I worked in the store in the wintertime because there wasn't a lot of ice cream sold, and people from everywhere came in there, and a lot of my classmates and their parents would come in there for want of a can of tuna, a can of salmon, or something. I used to feel so bad to say we don't have any. And my grandmother told me, said, "June, when it's somebody that's not your regular customer comes in and asks for one of those, bag of sugar or something, if you have it and you know that you do, but you don't for them, just cross your fingers and tell them you don't have it and real low say 'for you.'" So that made me feel better.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: But this was real funny, too. I jump from one thing to the other.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: That's all right.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: But in 1943, I would say was one of the worst years and early '44 on just practically everything that was either hard to get, couldn't get it, or just very, very, very scarce. And we were in a library at one of the sessions. I don't remember what. It might have been science or something. But anyway, my name came over the loud speaker to report to the office, and our principal at Bradley High was a former algebra teacher when I moved with grandmother and went to Allen School, but he was immediately then promoted to principal of Bradley High School and was principal there for many years. And I couldn't imagine what in the world. I thought, well, maybe something had happened to Uncle Van or my brother who was in a different school, maybe just something happened to him, just any number of things. Got in his office and he closed the door, and he wanted to talk to me about something, and his son was coming home the next week. He had been in Germany and was getting five days off because he had been injured and was going to get to come home for five days before he went back to Europe. And Mr. Kyle said Mrs. Kyle had been everywhere trying to find salmon for him, and said I know that (Vest) has a lot of special items, and wanted to know if I could please bring him a can of salmon to school and so his wife could make some salmon patties for the boy when he got home. And when I got ready to go out the door, he said now he would rather it just be our secret and not to mention it to anybody. You talk about feeling important, the next day I took him two cans of salmon. After that, I got calls just every so often. None of the classmates never did know what I was doing, except for my best friend, but it was real funny. But we had another attraction at the store, too. Bill's younger brother went to the Army. He was drafted, was stationed in Germany, and in 1943, it was probably a month and a half before Christmas, this huge, huge box arrived at the store for Bill, and it was all of this paraphernalia from Germany from Albert, and that was on a regular basis. We often wondered how in this world that he shipped those things out. But Bill took one of the old fashioned candy cases there at the store and displayed all that stuff that Albert sent, and there was guns, grenades. Everything was displayed in there.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Wow. Like you were in a museum there.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Uh-huh. Of course, they're all dead. The sons run the store today, all three of them. That's been their profession, and they were little boys when I started working.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: But it was real funny that--the way your life changes. You know, being so unhappy to move, and then being able to go to the store, and the store was not too far from where I had lived before, so I got to see all of my old friends and all of that. They were regular customers at the ice cream parlor in the summertime.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. But didn't you--I mean, didn't you feel like-- did you miss out on anything because you were working?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: I don't think anybody did. This is real strange, but in 2001, we had our 55th reunion for Bradley County High School of '46 and the final dinner was down here on the Southern Bell. We took--had a dinner cruise. And Bob Butler and myself were talking about it, and I said, "You know, I just always felt like our class was special because we graduated from grade school and the war happened, so all our years at high school was war years, and people--you didn't hear people complain." We complained more because the boys had to leave, and there wasn't too many boys left in town. All but everybody pitched in. I don't remember all my years, about four years of high school, of buying more than two or maybe three new books. There was a Coopers Bookstore on the town square there in Cleveland that everybody bought their books, and after we got our schedule, you know, with what we were taking, we bought used books. They had very few new books. There was some things like trigonometry, something that was most unusual, not an everyday subject, something like that you might have to buy a new book, but we went to Coopers Bookstore and bought our books for that year, and if--depended on how well that you took care of them, they were usually spoken for before school was out by somebody that was going to be in the year we were, behind us.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: And people just got used to sharing and helping any way they could, and remember, too, see, there was no TV's or anything then. It was strictly radio and movies. We went to the movies a lot in between time of going to classes and going to work just to see the news because we could see the national news at the Princess Theater.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. Is that, is that primarily how you kept up with what was going on in the war?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Uh-huh. News, newspapers, there was talk. You know, the day that Pearl Harbor was bombed was on a Sunday. It came on the radio. And, of course, everybody--my brother and my grandmother and myself, we were just stunned. It was just the three of us there getting ready to go to church. But when we got to church, there was no church and Sunday school classes. Everybody talked about the war, and there was prayers, and that's all it was. It was just talk because nobody knew except what had come on the national news. You know, on the radios, as to how it would effect us, what it was, how long it would last--

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: --and just how bad it was.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You've got to be kind of scared at that point, too, wondering--

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: I think everybody was. So you didn't really have time to think about what you didn't have or couldn't get. You were more concerned about what you could do to help the service men. Just like the victory gardens, as President Roosevelt called them, for--if everybody would, you know, make a garden, and then war bonds--I brought a war bond stamp book. I thought you might like to see that. Oh, there was drives, and I know I kept stacks of them by the cash register there at the store when this was going on that you could spend 18 dollars and 75 cents and fill that book of stamps. And take it to the bank and then you got a 25-dollar war bond. You could buy a 50-dollar war bond, it cost 37 dollars and 50 cents. I don't know why those figures stand out to me. I guess we had so many drives and went and bought so much because we would buy stamps. We had a certain day in school, all during my high school years, that it was stamp day. That you could buy stamps for war bonds because President Roosevelt needed any money that the American people would loan to the government. And then you got good interest on them, you know, if you kept them for the ten years to maturity. I know my daddy, we used to keep his war bonds in a locked thing in my special cedar chest. He had stacks of them, and people did. They had--everywhere that people worked, there was war bond drives. There was--you could say celebrities, singers and things like that that would go from town to town selling war bonds and promoting people to really get busy with them. In school, it worked out fine to have the books that you could fill up because you could spend a dollar a week and buy four quarter stamps. It wouldn't take too long, you would have a war bond.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: And then they had the 10-cent ones, too, the 10-cent stamps that you could buy and put in the--the books. I spent a lot of my money. I couldn't--I wasn't old enough to be on a payroll, so they worked it out that I would just help daddy make ice cream, and I helped him in the store some, but I spent just about everything that I made on stamps, on writing service men. I wrote an awful lot of boys.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: The man that I married, of course, he was my sweetheart, you know, before he left for the naval station. I wrote him every day.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hm. When did he go?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Pardon.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: When did he go to the naval station?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: He had to wait until he was 18. He went in '43. He graduated from high school when he was 16, in '42. He graduated from high school the year that I graduated from grade school. And he immediately signed up for--he wanted to be a pilot, and the principal and the teachers recommended him, his moral character and all, and he went to join the Navy. He was going to be a pilot, and he had to wait until he was 18. He couldn't, couldn't go when he was 16. He was 17 that summer after he graduated. So he got his orders October the 20th, 1943 and went through preflight school. I brought some of those letters that was real interesting. He mailed me an awfully lot of things that I'm sure that would be good for history today, books and things from different places. He went to five or six universities.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: While he was in the AFTC, the training program?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Oh, yeah, and got his gold wings in Clinton, Oklahoma, at the University of Oklahoma.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: When did--how long did it take him to do that? Do you remember?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: He went in in October of '43, and he got his Navy wings in November of '45. So it took over two years, but the letters were so interesting. I used to take some of his letters to school. Because it would be--their training that they went through, and I thought of--every time that George Bush Senior would talk about being in the Navy, I would think about some of those things that Ray would write home about the training and all that they had to go through, and I would say, "He was some man," because they washed out constantly in there.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You had to be pretty smart.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: You had to be smart to get in, and then to stay in, you really had to be smart because it was--

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Well, a lot of smart people were washing out, too. You had to be really coordinated.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: You had to, and then there was a place that--when he was at the University of Miami, he kept talking about this Venetian pool, and it was gigantic. It was just a huge, huge swimming pool, and they had to jump in, dive in from the driving board, take their shirt off, throw the shirt over their head, tie it up, and make a float out of it, and the same way with their pants. And the first time after we married, it was three, four years I guess after we married, we went down to see the Venetian pool, and it was just a regular swimming pool, regular sized swimming pool. We laughed about that for years because to a young boy, that was just--it was just gigantic. He kept talking about that biggest swimming pool he had ever seen. But he told all of those things that they did. That's why it was interesting. We used that in our history class in high school, a lot of times, parts of the letters that he wrote about.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Let me ask you this: After the war was over--I don't mean to jump forward, but I just want to ask you this question. After the war was over, when everybody was really pitching in and doing their part, and then the war is over, is there kind of a letdown that there's not the same sense of nationalism, pride, everyone pitching in? Did you kind of miss that?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: No, no, didn't, and we just didn't think about it or talk about it. Everybody was so busy getting on with the rest of their life because they felt like--I guess a lot of the boys felt like Ray did, that his life had been distracted, and he did it for his country, and he was so busy with getting on with the rest of his life, we were just always really busy people.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What about looking back at it though, do you find yourself--

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Look back for years at all that stuff had been sealed up and packed up and if anybody asked things--and then two of his real good friends were buddies that got their wings when Ray got his. One lived in Washington state and one in Indiana. We visited with them throughout the years, and they did with us in Chattanooga. But, no, I don't--there was some, some people that got shell shocked and had depression, but I think a lot of that depended on the person, and maybe all of the trauma and all that they actually went through.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: People saw some pretty horrible things.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: My uncle didn't see the actual war, but he said the people in India, I know he went and had--he just had a hard time adjusting to civilian life when he came back because he was so used to that group of people that he said was so pitiful and just from a lot--and must have been just a mass amount of little children that were malnourished--

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Diseased.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: --diseased and all of that. And it really got next to him. The first thing he said when he got home, that he was never going to marry, never going to have any children. He was never going to bring any children into the world to ever be subject to anything like that. And he met this girl and married and had a little girl.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Had a girl?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Yeah. We used to kid him about that. But, gosh, all of those people, just about, they were a big part of my childhood are dead because they were, you know, older than I was, and I believe that there is one lady--my brother lives in Cleveland today. He has a business there. He just--you couldn't talk to him about moving anywhere outside of Cleveland. He's there to stay, been there for years, but he goes over in the old neighborhood that we grew up in and there was one lady that was a friend of mother's, and he said that she is still living. And he went by to see her one day. She's 90--I believe he told me she was 96 years old. I talked to him the other day, and he calls me every so often to see what--something that happened because I always kept diaries and scrapbooks and notes from anything that we ever did from the time I was a little bitty girl. I don't know why. I just always have liked that part of living.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So when the war is over, everything starts--kind of gets back to getting normal. All right. The men start getting back into town. At that time you had been writing your future husband for--all the time, right?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: I wrote him every day and sometimes twice a day.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hm. So I mean--

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: All of those years that I was in high school, from the time he left in 1943, every day, and as I said, sometimes twice a day because in the different classes they were in, there was certain times the postman ran. I know in two or three of his letters, he said, "I received your letter this morning, and, hopefully, I'll get another one this afternoon," but he didn't settle for one or two a week. I mean, it was every day. He wanted to know everything I did. But, as I said, we were real young, and that was a different experience for him.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: But it was--it was understood that there was a relationship though. Right?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You were waiting for him. Right?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Uh-huh, and I couldn't even date. That's what's so funny.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Do you think that makes the relationship stronger then? That's probably--you were probably keeping him sane, to some extent. Right?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Probably.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did he talk about that much?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Yeah. It was comical.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: You know, but I know he would have watch, and he explained in one of the letters, he said, now, what you know is watch, it's not like a soldier walking back and forth with a gun patrolling. We watch the dorm, and we're at a desk. The only thing is we can't go to sleep. And he had a 12-hour duty that night. So he wrote me two letters during the night while he was waiting until 6:00 the next morning. But this was, this amazed me on one of the paragraphs he was talking about patrolling the barracks, and two of his buddies three nights before had decided, well, they would just go to sleep. There was nothing going on. Nobody was outside and all, and they got kicked out of naval aviation, and he said had it been--had they been in a war zone, they would have been shot as traitors.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Wow. Had it been a war zone, they probably wouldn't have done it that way.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: I don't think they would have, but maybe that's what they told them.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: But, you know, I thought, gosh, in America, they surely wouldn't shoot them for dozing off to sleep, but they, they did things just like you would if you were, you know, on patrol, except you were at a desk in the front of the building in the office all night.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And you didn't get to see him at all during the war?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Oh, yes. He came home.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, he did get to come home.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Yeah. Daddy wouldn't let me go visit him. I wanted to really bad. Daddy thought I'd lost my ever-loving mind. That little boy is a man, and you're not about to go. But when he got his wings, I had started on daddy like I did for him to let me go to work, that I want to go to Clinton, Oklahoma. I offered to take I don't know how many women with me, and no. We always had to make ice cream, or they couldn't do without me. But you talk about after the war when Ray got his--he was never discharged as such. He just was put on inactive duty from naval aviation.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Uh-huh. When we set our wedding date, the people from the store, the customers, throughout the four years of high school and all, they--we used to eat and try different things, vegetables and all that. And one woman in particular was always willing to do some special cooking, and we would get some real pretty vegetables in that just looked like they might be good, and she was forever trying something. So I got more recipes and more unusual things for wedding gifts than you could shake a stick at.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How soon after he got back did you set a wedding date?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How soon?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: He got back in May of '46, and we married in November of '46. We set a date on Thanksgiving day. We were trying to have something different, and we were gonna have a church wedding. My grandmother had been a member of that Big Springs Baptist Church ever since she had resided in Cleveland. The pastor was originally from LaFayette, Georgia. That's why my grandmother had moved to Cleveland. And there had never been a wedding at that church. So that's where we decided to have it after the sunrise service on Thanksgiving morning. My grandmother, unbeknown to us, had issued a blanket invitation the Sunday before. So when the wedding party got there, there was no place to sit. Everybody had came to the sunrise service and nobody left.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Funny.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: It's funny now, and it was funny after it was over with, but at that time it was almost devastating, goodness gracious, but they were just curious, as I said having never had a church service wedding there, to see what it would be, I guess. I don't know. I was just scared to death. Good gracious.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you got married then in November of '46.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And you were--

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: I was 18.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: --18. And what did you end up doing? Did you stay in Cleveland?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: We stayed in Cleveland until--Ray, in the meantime, when he was waiting to get 18, his dad owned a service station, and he had worked at the service station for him and bought parts over at a place in Cleveland. So while he was waiting to go into the Navy, he went to work at that Hearts Auto Parts there in Cleveland, as well as helping his daddy at the service station. So when he got out of service, they had wrote him and wanted him to come to work for Hearts as a salesman, and he went to work for them. And in the meantime, a manager wasn't doing any good in Calhoun, Georgia. So Henry asked Ray to go in as manager in Calhoun, Georgia, in '47, provided that we could both go to Calhoun, Georgia, and not let on at all about our age because the assistant manager was in his 50's, and he said that it just wouldn't sit well with the people there, and it was a little store next to the courthouse there in downtown Calhoun, Georgia. And we moved to Calhoun in '47, in the spring of '47.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Um--

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: And stayed there for two years, and the store just--it--the town wasn't big enough to have two parts stores, and there was another part store there and Hearts. So they talked about it and decided to close the store down, and Ray traveled for them as a traveling salesman.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What about when the Korean War broke out? Did he get a letter?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: No. He was in the--just a reserve unit down at Market Street Bridge, but, no, he didn't go to the--anything except during World War II.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So then after you left Calhoun, did you come back to base--

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: We come back to Cleveland, and then from Cleveland, he went with another company as a traveling salesman in Chattanooga with Sharp Automotive.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you continue to work after you got married?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: No. Bill--they--he and my dad had big plans for my life, and I had different plans, so--

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Well, I was supposed to go to college, and I was going to be the envious of anybody that came to the grocery store, my office and all that I would have, and I would oversee that they were going to put most stores in Cleveland, and that could have interested me least of all of anything.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What about your little brother?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: My little brother was--went in the Army when he was 16. My dad signed for him to go to the Army. We came home from Calhoun, came to Cleveland one weekend. My brother wasn't there, and I got really upset at my dad for putting him in the Army. But Bob didn't like school. He was as dissatisfied as I was after mom died and we moved to grandmother's, but we just showed it in different ways. Being a boy, he didn't work or anything. I got mine from--my steam off from working and doing all types of anything I could do to help the war effort. And Bob was still in school, had to go to school, disliked it. And they passed a new law. I haven't ever checked on that. In fact, Bob asked me if I knew what law daddy was talking about two or three weeks ago when I was talking to him. I said, "You know, that's one thing I never did check on." But daddy told me and Ray that the government had passed a new law when--it was '47 when he went in--that if the parent would sign for it, a 16-year old could go in peacetime, and the Army was guaranteed to make a man out of a boy. And Bob had played hooky so much from school and had spent a big part of his time in the theater there in Cleveland and at that pool hall and all, and daddy just signed him up for the Army. According to daddy, Bob wanted to go. Bob said, "Yeah, I wanted to go to the Army as bad as you wanted to go to work." So he went to the Army and stayed, and he got out in '50, '50-something and got married. He went to Alaska, stayed in Alaska for a long time and then got in the insurance business when he got out and then became a local merchant, and he's been in that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: In Alaska?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: No, in Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: When he got--

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How did he end up in Alaska?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: The Army sent him there.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: And he took his new wife. He met, he met Phyllis when he was home on furlough before he was going to Alaska. And they only--he only knew her about a week, and they got married, came to Chattanooga for me to take him down to the train station and then would I take Phyllis back home. That's the first time I knew that he was married. And she is one of the sweetest sister-in-laws you've ever seen. And she's retired from insurance business and helps him there in the store. They both retired, but he won't ever retire. He's got--he's one--he's like me. He's got to be doing something all the time, as long as he's got the store and sees people, and they come in. He sells a good line of vacuum cleaners, two or three types of vacuums, all types of sewing machines, does all types of repairs, and all that. And if you're ever in Cleveland, he's in the middle of Keith Street Plaza, which is one of the main streets there in Cleveland. It's Southern Sewing Machine Company. He would be delighted for you to come in and see him. He has people just every now and then that I have run into that have been through there and say he always calls me. If some of them--he knows a lot of my classmates, high school classmates, and they stop in to see him. Several of them are customers of his that's bought vacuum cleaners or sewing machines. But I hadn't lived in Cleveland since '47.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Where are you now?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Chattanooga.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: We moved to Chattanooga in 1950.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Let me ask you this: How do you think this generation--later generations, but we'll talk about this one--how do you think they would react to a situation where they were asked to ration, make the sacrifices, the draft? Do you think they would deal with the--deal with it--

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: I believe it would be most difficult for them to do that because I think if you think about it each, each generation wants your children to have it a little easier than what they did, and so many of them aren't taught that. And I think in today's world, so many of the men and women are both working and the children, their family, is a secondary thing.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. That's true. And plus the World War II generation had just come off the Depression, and they were __+.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: That's true. And I think that had a lot to do with the boys because I know people have asked Ray many times because from the time he was a little boy, he had wanted to fly, and he used to have play airplanes and all of that, as to why did you not become a commercial pilot, since you wanted to fly, and not only him, but I think a lot felt the same way, that the war came along at a time in their life where they were just getting ready to live and something they had to do, and they wanted as far away from it as they could get. And in letters that I was reading not long ago from his two best friends, each one of them felt the same way, except they each went back to school. Ray didn't. He said he'd had all the school that he ever wanted because he went to so many universities, and I couldn't imagine a naval pilot going back to school, and one of them, the one from Indiana, was going to one of the schools that they had went to when they was in the Navy. You see a lot of those, a lot of businesses and all changed into something else during the war and I know a lot of the colleges became, became hospitals throughout the United States.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. And they, a lot of the courses, the classes that they were taking were kind of set up so that you get them through.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So you were learning twice as much material in half the time.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: In fact, as you say, a lot of people were washing out.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Mm-hm. On the celestial navigation, on that thing, on being a navigator, it was trigonometry, algebra, all of that stuff, and just massive amounts, massive doses of courses, eight hours a day. So it was a very rigid thing. You could--you read some of those letters, and you say, well, how some would flunk out, particularly if they didn't have a lot of stamina to begin with--well, they would have to have a certain amount to get in there, but they went through an awful lot to get those, those gold wings.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hm. Do you take the opportunity--take any opportunities to enlighten younger generations about the kind much sacrifices you went through, the kind of things that really everyone was doing during that time? Have you had that opportunity?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: You know, it has never come up. I talk a lot. I've been active in garden clubs and all that for all my adult life, beautification projects in the city and all that, but as far as taking it as a subject to talk about, it was just--

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No, just taking the opportunity to tell. I think the reason I asked because really the reason for this project, I think generations don't really understand the sacrifices--

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: --that were made. They don't realize, and their whole perception is from the movies. They get--you know, their idea of what was going on is from the movies, and you don't see a lot about the home front. You don't see a lot about the sacrifices that were being made back here at home.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Well, you know, you used to stand in line to get a pair of hose, silk hose. That was just one of the things that was a shortage of, and you do wonder, well, what would the generation of today do if they couldn't go to the store and buy a particular kind of sock or a particular type of shoe and all that they like, and then if a store did get them in, that they would have to stand in line. Hopefully they wouldn't sell out before they get there. Looking back now, you think about those things, but, yet, at the time we didn't think anything about it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. That's really where I was going. During the time you don't even think about it as a sacrifice.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Huh-uh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You just think about it that's the way it is.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: That's the way it is. The biggest sacrifice of all was the men having to go to service. So the ones left at home would do anything they could to help the men.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Do you look back over the time fondly then, over the, over the time that you spent? You were working really hard and everyone was pitching in, but do you look back fondly over that?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I met so many people, and I enjoyed doing what I was doing. It just--as I said, I just never thought about it. And I guess, there again, it depends on the attitude that a person has, but I just was just so glad to get something to do. I had begged and pleaded to worked so bad.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So we've got a few more minutes left. Is there anything you would like to talk about that we didn't cover in the interview?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: I think not only myself, but I would think a lot of people that in learning to substitute things helped me tremendously in my adult life, so if you run out of something, and you was cooking dinner, and having some special people over for dinner that night and you accidentally run out of something, it was no big deal. You would substitute something to do that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. Because you couldn't __+.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Nothing __+.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: As I said, you just didn't think about it. But my grandmother's faith in her church I think had an awful lot to do with the, the boys' safety and all of that because it--she was--if ever there was a faithful woman--see, not only that, then she had another one of her sons go to the Army, too, and he had three children--

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: --when he left.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was that World War II or Korea?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: World War II. You had to register, and then they started out with all the single boys, then it started out with married men with one child, then the married men with two children, then the married men with three children. And Uncle Wilson fell in that category in '43 with--I still think that was the most crucial year because there's a lot of things that happened in '43.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: They were getting ready for D-Day, too.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Uh-huh. He happened to fall in that category, and his wife was expecting the fourth child.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, my goodness. Was he okay?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Oh, yeah. He went to Italy. But looking back, you know, I--I think that that church--not only grandmother's church, but churches across the United States, I think that the, the people really--they did a lot to promote patriotism, and all of the ministers and all would just like for you to have meatless days. They come up with having one meatless day, and everybody would have a meatless day. You just wouldn't dare think about sitting down and eating meat on that meatless day because that helped the service men.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: And I know in making ice cream, the mix, we get the bought mix, those great big, I guess, 25-gallon cans or something already with everything in it, except the color of chocolate or strawberry and flavorings and things like that. It got real, real scarce. Daddy and Bill used to sit down there at one of the tables in the ice cream parlor, and they'd figured what they could do to stretch something to still have customers coming in. And they came up with the idea that they would make sherbert. We had great big long trays that you froze the ice cream sherbert, which is made with water, and dump it out and cut it up in little squares. Then make the vanilla ice cream. While you put in cartons, put so much of the vanilla ice cream in, and then you'd put a little square of the orange sherbert in the middle then fill it up with vanilla ice scream, and we could get twice as many quarts of ice treatment out of so much ice cream mix than we could to just make pure vanilla ice cream. That was one of the biggest sellers. Then when it got really scarce--

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Just like a creamsicle, right?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: It's like the creamsicles today, except this you spooned out of--we didn't have much of anything like that. We made ice cream sandwiches and then started making fudgesicles, not fudgesicles but brown cows. I did a little bit of all that. See, we made the ice cream right here at the end of one of the counters. It was a great big ice cream parlor. You stepped down two steps from the grocery store. And the cash register was up here in the grocery store. And then you step down, there's two steps, and here was a great big ice cream parlor with a bunch of stools down by the counter and then so many tables out front, so being by the cash register, that was why it was real easy for me to run up the steps and wait on customers in the store, and then anybody in the ice cream parlor, I ran back down the steps, thought no more about it than nothing, just--I've got two pictures in there I want you to see. You won't believe it. That's what I was looking for a while ago. As I said, I have--is the tape finished?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No. Go ahead and pull the pictures.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Pull pictures? Let's see.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yes. We have a few minutes left.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Okay. This, I just thought you would get a kick out of this, but which one is it? Maybe it's this one. You know, we've become such creatures of habit, don't we? Having things fixed a certain way, and then change it and decide, well, that's all wrong. I believe it's in this one. Oh, this is what I wanted you to see, too. I think you would appreciate that. I'm finding everything except for what I want to find. You said the tape is about finished?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah. You've got about a minute left. Okay. Explain what that picture is.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: This is a picture of me in front of the ice cream parlor.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Pull back just a little. There you go.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: I was about 15 years old.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Is that while, while your future husband is off at war?

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Yes. He was in training to be a pilot.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Here you go. Pull back. There you go. That's fine.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: Is that okay?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah. I just want to take the time to thank you for coming down here. I appreciate you __.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: I had made a bunch of these there on the picture maker, and took them to our class reunion to give the brother, Bobby, the one that--I think he has cancer, the one that his picture was made in front of the ice cream parlor. His daddy had promised him a bicycle for his birthday. So he was so proud to get it, and came running over to the store on his bicycle for me to take a picture of him on his new bicycle. I took three or four pictures of him, but Jimmy really-- well, the class really all got a kick out of it, you know, when they saw it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Five seconds left on the tape.

sp.speaker: June Delay Tallent
sp.p: This you might want to see, too.
